This study focuses on the control of the active power in the power system; hence, for a simpler presen- tation, we do not define the reactive power representations for these loads and sources. In this power system, the BESS units are to be operated in GFL mode when the data center is grid connected, and they would be used to provide a reduction in the demand of utility power from the data center by discharging the BESS upon request of the utility. For the rare cases of a loss of utility power, the BESS units would be operated in GFM mode to provide stable backup power to the data center loads. For longer-duration utility outages, the generators would ramp up as the stored energy of the BESS units deplete. When the utility power returns, the data center would reconnect to the power grid, and the BESS would recharge to its target SOC. The PFMS, described in the next section, is responsible for coordinating the various assets in the data center power system to accomplish the desired operational behavior described here. 7 This report is available at no cost from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) at www.nrel.gov/publications Figure2.Conceptualsingle-linediagramofthedatacenterpowersystem 8 This report is available at no cost from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) at www.nrel.gov/publications 4 Power Flow Management System The PFMS is a secondary control system responsible for ensuring stable, uninterrupted power delivery to the loads in the data center and for using the data center assets, such as the BESS, to respond to requests from the grid. The PFMS is critical to ensuring the stability of the data center power system while im- proving the resilience of the grid by responding to utility dispatch requests. The stable power delivery to loads requires the PFMS to constantly monitor the status of the grid, BESS, generators, and loads, and decide on the control actions/sequences of operation to be executed. The design of the PFMS is based on open standards, such as IEEE 2030.7 and IEEE 1547-2018; and it uses standard communication inter- faces, such as Modbus Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), DNP3, and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) 61850. It monitors and controls power hardware, such as the BESS, generators, and relays; and it can also interface with higher-level systems, such as supervisory control and data acquisition systems and advanced distribution management systems.
